"Each year, Australia faces increasingly unprecedented wildfires, marked both by their scale and by the intense public disagreements about their political, cultural, and ecological causes. How to Control Fire on a Burning Continent is a critical and ethnographic exploration of wildfire management in Australia and the technoscientific systems of control that shape its current and future possibilities. Timothy Neale observes how two seemingly opposing forces—an entrenched sense of crisis and widespread normalization—combine to form an apparatus of institutional fire management that increasingly centers technical control and militarization. While sympathetic to the double binds many fire management professionals find themselves in, Neale ties contemporary wildfire problems to ongoing colonization and Indigenous dispossession, exploring Indigenous-led land management and cultural burning as a practical assertion of sovereignty. Inside the high-tech, collaborative plan to extinguish the Brassknocker fire

By Jimmy Parker
Updated January 12 2026 - 7:47pm, first published 7:40pm

Chris Allen knows that for a community scarred by Black Summer, every new plume of smoke feels like a recurring nightmare.
The Far South Coast RFS district manager wanted to reassure the community that the Brassknocker fire was very different this time around, and was determined to ensure the ending was different, too.

The bushfire is located north of Yowrie, south of Belowra, and about 20 kilometres north-west of Cobargo in Wadbilliga National Park.
"The anxiety of 2019-20, Coolagolite, Yankees Gap and Tathra, is at the forefront of our minds," Mr Allen told ACM's Bega District News.
But he assured people, "The fire scar is very, very different from Black Summer.
"The fuel load is very different. The water accessibility is very different to what we had to deal with. We have evolved and we are a better collaborative fire service than what we were, with aviation and heavy plant support.

"We are one of the major fires in the state at the moment as opposed to 2019-20, so resource availability is so much better, and while it is going to be a durational fire, it's not something that should be compared."
As Rural Fire Service incident controller, Mr Allen is keeping a close eye on how the Brassknocker Trail fire is developing.
"The identified area goes from the Snowy Monaro local government boundary to the west, Dignams Creek to the north, the Princes Highway to the east, and the Snowy Mountains Highway to the south," Mr Allen said.
"Looking at the footprint and aerial images that we've just seen through the fire camera, there's a lot of hotspots, there's no running fire, but obviously the conditions are quite benign at the moment.

The operabackburningstudy in collaboration. Personnel were divided between observing real-time aerial footage, studying updated cartographic data in both physical and digital formats, and managing direct telecommunications from the fireground.
Mr Allen said there were 48 trucks on site with Forestry NSW crews from the North Coast, and National Parks and Wildlife Service and RFS teams predominantly from the Far South Coast.

The incident controller said parts of the fire were being actively suppressed by water,while other areas were being suppressed through intentionally placed fire or backburns.
He also noted that any fire added would have the support of "water-bucketing" to control its spread.
"The backburning operations that we are doing is quite strategic," Mr Allen said.
"It isn't close backburning as we are away from the actual fire and is well inside the current footprint of where we expect it to end up.

"Some of the backburning will be done vehicle-based, while others will be done via helicopter incendiaries and we've identified ridges where the fire can burn downhill."
Mr Allen confirmed on January 12 that the fire was not going to be contained within the next three to four days.
"It's a large fire in remote country and it is going to take a lot of time and patience, but we're confident of a good outcome," he said.

Indigenous advice helps firefighters

Mr Allen said the collaborative firefighting effort included Merrimans Local Aboriginal Land Council which had been feeding information as part of the strategic planning process.

"On that bad fire day, there were five to six questions we went to them and they were able to be part of the decision-making: where we were pulling water from, where we can put a dozer line," Mr Allen said.
"I've never worked in an incident management team that's had this much involvement from our local land council, and my dream is that this becomes a bit of a norm.
"I can't thank them enough."

@SuperMoosie And here's a really important detail that people reading this who don't live in Sydney might not appreciate.

Usually, when you say "outer suburbs", people assume one- or two-storey detached single family homes.

In Sydney, our outer suburbs have apartments.

As in, the outermost suburbs of Sydney, like Asquith, Hornsby, and Mount Colah, have apartment buildings.

To put that in context for Melburnians: Imagine an outer suburb near a national park, like Upwey or Belgrave, with multiple five-to-10 floor apartment buildings. That's Asquith.

Imagine multiple apartment towers going up on new subdivisions in Pakenham. That's Rouse Hill.

There are new subdivisions in suburbs like Rouse Hill that have apartments.

You can quite comfortably walk from the Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (which is the big national park just north of Sydney) to an apartment block.

(When people in the Inner West complain about new apartment blocks impacting the amenity and feel of their neighbourhood, it leads to more people living in apartment blocks on the outer fringe.)

These outer suburban blocks are really quite common in Sydney. More so than most other Australian or North American cities.

So the risks associated with a large bushfire spotting embers 1km to 2km from a national park on the urban fringe are an order of magnitude greater in Sydney than other metro areas.

Guidelines for Small Kennel Quilts:

Materials used should be 100% cotton (biodegradable) on the advice of a veterinarian. This includes the fabric, batting, and thread. Do not use fleece for it sheds to much. Do not use flannel for it often has synthetic fibers. Even 100% cotton flannel tends to pill and it is not suitable for Kennel Quilts during a disaster. Terry Cloth is not suitable for Kennel Quilts. Little claws can catch on it. Batting cannot have scrim for scrim is usually made of polyester. This is a safety issue in case the pet chews the Kennel Quilt.
You do not have to prewash the fabric, but wash the Kennel Quilt after it is made. (pets can have allergies just like humans).
Finished size should be 12" x 18". This fits the most commonly used small kennel used at shelters.
When piecing, use a small stitch length (e.g. 14 stitches/inch).
Do not use binding as it can be hazardous to pets if it becomes loose. Layer, sew around the edge using a small stitch length, and turn quilts pillow-cover style. Whipstitch the opening with small, tight stitches.
Use only simple appliques that are secured with tight stitches along the edges. Avoid using fusibles.
Keep the quilting simple and use small tight quilting stitches that won’t catch on pet claws. Do not tie quilts as the ends can get caught in claws or chewed off.
Do not use any metallic threads or other embellishments (e.g. beads, charms, buttons, ribbons, lace, trims, etc.) of any kind. Do not add handles or loops to the quilt.

World Chimpanzee Day

Il 14 luglio torna il World Chimpanzee Day, la giornata mondiale dedicata agli scimpanzé: geni della foresta, acrobati del buonumore e, diciamolo, i più irresistibili “quasi-umani” del pianeta. Dal 2018 questa ricorrenza celebra l’eredità di Jane Goodall, che proprio il 14 luglio del 1960 mise piede nella foresta di Gombe e cambiò per sempre la storia della biologia. Da allora, ogni anno, il mondo si riunisce per festeggiare i nostri parenti più stretti con iniziative, scoperte e un bel po’ di risate.

✨ Novità 2026: cosa bolle nella giungla?

Il tema internazionale di quest’anno è “Voices of the Forest”, un invito a dare spazio — e volume — alle storie degli scimpanzé, dei ricercatori e dei santuari che li proteggono. E le novità non mancano:

  • Nuova mappa globale dei santuari: il Jane Goodall Institute ha lanciato una piattaforma interattiva che permette di “visitare” virtualmente i centri di recupero in Africa, con video in diretta delle attività quotidiane dei chimp (spoiler: sì, litigano per le banane).
  • Progetto ChimpanZoom 2.0: un upgrade del programma educativo che porta nelle scuole europee lezioni immersive in realtà aumentata. I bambini potranno osservare come gli scimpanzé costruiscono nidi, comunicano e… rubano frutta con una destrezza degna di un ladro di scena.
  • Campagna #BananaForChange: influencer, biologi e artisti uniti per sensibilizzare sulla perdita dell’habitat. L’idea? Trasformare la banana in simbolo di protezione ambientale. Preparati a vedere stories gialle ovunque.
  • Nuovi dati scientifici: nel 2026 è stato pubblicato uno studio che conferma che gli scimpanzé non solo usano strumenti, ma li modificano in base al contesto. In pratica: piccoli MacGyver della savana.

💚🤍❤️E in Italia?

Il 2026 segna un boom di iniziative:

  • I bioparchi di Roma, Ravenna e Verona ospitano laboratori “chimp-lab” per bambini, con attività di problem solving ispirate alle tecniche degli scimpanzé.
  • Il Centro di Monte Adone presenta il progetto “Scimmie in Ascolto”, dedicato alla riabilitazione comportamentale degli animali salvati dal traffico illegale.
  • Sui social italiani spopola il filtro “Chimp Chic”, che trasforma il volto degli utenti in una versione scimmiesca glamour (non sempre lusinghiera, ma decisamente divertente).

🎉 Perché festeggiare?

Perché gli scimpanzé sono in pericolo, ma anche pieni di vita, cultura, emozioni e sorprese. Ridono, ballano sotto la pioggia, si offendono se ignorati e condividono con noi il 98,7% del DNA. Celebrarli significa ricordare che proteggere loro è proteggere anche noi.

Bill Helin is of #Tsimshian / #Norwegian decent and is a member of the Tsimshian Nation, born and raised in the Northwest Coastal community of Prince Rupert, BC. His father was Arthur Helin, his Grandfather Henry William Helin, was Chief of the Gitlan Tribe, and his Grandmother Maud Helin, was Chief of the Gitgeese Tribe. Bill spent many hours listening to his grandmother in wonder, as she told him many Legends of the Tsimshian People. By the time he was three, he was already drawing and it wasn't long before he was amusing his family, friends and teachers with caricatures and cartoons. For the most part Bill is a self-taught artist. He learned from books, and was soon mastering techniques such as three-dimensional forming, called repousse. In the 1980’s Bill was sponsored to go to K'San, BC's famous #IndianArt and Carving School in Hazelton. In February 1988, Bill attended the renowned Gemology Institute of America in Santa Monica, California, completing advanced courses in gold smithing and gem setting. Today he lives and works from his studio/home on Vancouver Island.

Bill spent most of his career, which started in 1979, carving traditional Tsimshian wood carving, jewelry and paintings. His art has evolved from creating large wood projects such as a 40 foot long Ravensong Canoe in 1993 and working on the world’s tallest totem pole with Richard Krentz in 1994, to illustrating children’s story books and working on many animation projects. Other projects include working with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency to design three mission patches as well as some education materials.

Yesterday morning, a bird brained itself against one of our windows.
Mrs Blackbird was very stunned, and tried to hide in the grass. I kept her safe from inquisitive cats for an hour, but she wasn’t going anywhere - so I put her in a cat carrier, brought her inside and kept her safe and warm.
I wasn’t hopeful, but this morning she suddenly awoke, ate all the food I had left her, and was hopping around.
#WildlifeRescue #WestCork

I opened her box, she flew off towards the trees from whence the other had called. Hopefully reunited with her mate who’d been searching for her.

It’s a good day.

We went for a kayak on the Mystic River on this ridiculously beautiful day and found this owl stuck in a tree, its wing tip ensnared in fishing line. People on the shore were making calls for wildlife rescue, so we left the scene.
1/2

#kayaking #BarredOwl #WildlifeRescue

When we returned front a jaunt up the Alewife Brook, the people had left but the owl was still there. 😢 So we called Mass Wildlife and reported it while we ate our sandwiches. When we circled back, the people were back and said Arlington animal rescue said they were coming, but it had been an hour. We were going back, but Mass Wildlife called back to say they couldn't send anybody for a while and that we should try Arlington, too.
2/3

So back again to update the folks on the bank.
It was then that we decided we should just try to do it ourselves.
Success! We managed to get all the line untangled. The owl will need to do some preening, but its wing seemed to work fine (folded it up lickety spit as soon as the first line was cut and no flesh wounds.) And no humans were injured in the effort.
He didn't fly off right away, but we figured he'd rather we all go away.
